result: The authors establish a zebrafish larval model of S. Typhimurium persistent infection by injecting bacteria into the hindbrain ventricle (HBV), demonstrating dose-dependent outcomes including high proliferation (47% mortality), persistent infection (40% of survivors with 10-2000 CFU), and bacterial clearance (36% of survivors), with bacteria persisting up to 14 days post-infection.
evaluation: Claims C15-C19 and C70 provide comprehensive experimental evidence including survival curves, CFU counts, and imaging data across multiple time points (Figures 1C-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). The dose-response relationship is well-characterized with appropriate controls (PBS injection), and the three distinct infection outcomes are clearly defined and quantified. The model successfully demonstrates bacterial persistence, which is the primary goal stated in C61.

result: Salmonella HBV infection induces a biphasic inflammatory response in zebrafish larvae: an early pro-inflammatory phase (3 hpi) characterized by elevated expression of il-1b, tnfa, tnfb, il-8, mmp9, and ccl38a.4 (CCL2), followed by decreased expression at 1 dpi, then re-elevation at 2-4 dpi. The macrophage marker mfap4 is upregulated throughout infection while mpeg1 is downregulated.
evaluation: Claims C20-C24 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing temporal gene expression patterns with appropriate statistical analysis (n=8 replicates, Kruskal-Wallis test). The biphasic inflammatory response is clearly demonstrated with significant changes at multiple time points. The CCL2/CCR2 axis involvement is supported by both experimental data and citation (C22, Cambier et al., 2014). The mpeg1 downregulation is confirmed by prior literature (Benard et al., 2015).

result: During early Salmonella infection (3 hpi to 16 hpi), both macrophages and neutrophils are recruited to the HBV infection site and actively phagocytose bacteria. Macrophages show sustained recruitment through 4 dpi with myelopoiesis, and macrophage depletion experiments demonstrate that macrophages are essential for controlling infection, as depletion increases mortality from 4% to 54% and leads to systemic bacterial dissemination.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by comprehensive imaging data (Figures 3A-H, Videos 1-4) including light sheet microscopy, confocal microscopy, and 3D reconstructions showing leukocyte recruitment and phagocytosis. The macrophage depletion experiments (C28-C29, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F-H) provide functional evidence with appropriate controls (MTZ treatment, NTR transgenic system). Quantification shows significant differences with proper statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test, n values reported). The conclusion in C116 is well-supported by the depletion data.

result: At late stages of infection (4 dpi), Salmonella persists primarily within large clusters of macrophages in the HBV, with 60% of recruited macrophages harboring bacteria. Macrophage recruitment is five times stronger at 4 dpi compared to 16 hpi. In contrast, few neutrophils are present at 4 dpi, they are not clustered, and do not contain persistent bacteria.
evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by high-resolution confocal imaging and 3D reconstructions (Figures 4A-G, Video 5) showing bacterial localization within macrophages. Quantification data (Figures 4F, 5A) demonstrate the five-fold increase in macrophage recruitment and the 60% infection rate among macrophages at 4 dpi. The contrast with neutrophils (C33) is clearly shown in Figures 4C-D. Multiple replicates are pooled (n=20-43 embryos) with appropriate statistical tests.

result: During early infection (first hours), up to 80% of macrophages polarize toward M1-like phenotype (tnfa-positive), including both infected and bystander macrophages. At late stages (4 dpi), macrophages switch phenotype with less than 10% remaining tnfa-positive, and persistent Salmonella are found within tnfa-negative (non-M1) macrophages.
evaluation: Claims C36-C39 are supported by time-lapse imaging using dual transgenic reporters Tg(mfap4:mCherry-F/tnfa:GFP-F) (Figures 6A-F, Videos 6-7). Quantification shows clear temporal dynamics with 80% M1 polarization early and <10% at 4 dpi (Figure 6B, F). The localization of bacteria in tnfa-negative macrophages is demonstrated by 3D reconstruction (Figure 6E). Statistical analysis includes appropriate sample sizes (n=12-23 larvae) and tests (one sample Wilcoxon test). The phenotypic switch described in C111 is well-documented.

result: Transcriptomic profiling of FACS-sorted macrophages reveals highly dynamic gene expression during infection. At 4 hpi, M1-activated macrophages show 3173 upregulated and 2847 downregulated genes with enrichment in pro-inflammatory pathways (TNF, cytokines, chemotaxis, complement). At 4 dpi, non-M1 macrophages show only 104 upregulated and 440 downregulated genes specific to this state, with enrichment in anti-inflammatory/pro-regenerative genes and cell adhesion pathways.
evaluation: Claims C40-C50 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis (Figure 7, Figure 7—source data 1) with appropriate experimental design (4 replicates per condition, DESeq2 analysis, p-adj <0.05). FACS gating strategy is clearly documented (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) showing 92.5% M1 at 4 hpi and 80.9% non-M1 at 4 dpi. Cell purity is confirmed by marker gene expression (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3). GO and KEGG pathway analyses support the functional interpretations. The dramatic difference in DEG numbers (6020 at 4 hpi vs 544 at 4 dpi) supports the conclusion of highly dynamic signatures (C117-C118).

result: Macrophages do not express wt1b at 4 hours post-infection but strongly express wt1b at 4 days post-infection, with large clusters of wt1b-positive macrophages harboring persistent bacteria.
evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by confocal imaging of Tg(mfap4:mCherry-F/wt1b:GFP-F) larvae (Figure 8A-D) showing clear temporal differences in wt1b expression. The imaging provides direct visual evidence of the phenotypic switch, and the observation of wt1b-positive macrophage clusters with bacteria at 4 dpi validates the transcriptomic findings (C47) regarding pro-regenerative marker expression.

result: Cell adhesion genes are differentially regulated during infection with distinct signatures between acute and persistent phases. Macrophage motility is enhanced at 1 hpi with increased migration speed, but at 4 dpi motility is dramatically reduced with very short trajectories. Both bystander and infected macrophages show reduced velocity during persistent infection (4 dpi), forming clusters of motionless macrophages that provide a niche for Salmonella.
evaluation: Claims C52-C58 are supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of adhesion-related genes (Figure 9A) and by trajectory tracking experiments (Figures 9B-D, Videos 8-9). Quantification shows statistically significant differences in macrophage velocity between time points and between bystander vs infected macrophages (n=76-195 tracks, t-test and Kruskal-Wallis test). The correlation between reduced adhesion gene expression, decreased motility, and bacterial persistence (C120) is logically coherent and supported by the data.

result: Neutrophil velocity is increased at 1 hpi but unchanged at 4 dpi compared to controls, and neutrophil velocity is consistently higher than macrophage velocity in all conditions. This differential motility pattern suggests that cell density does not affect leukocyte motility during persistent infection.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by neutrophil tracking data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test). The observation that neutrophils maintain normal mobility while macrophages become stationary (C121) provides evidence against cell density as the limiting factor. However, C121 is an inference that could benefit from additional experimental validation, though it is reasonable given the data.

result: During persistent infection, bacteria survive inside non-inflammatory macrophages that accumulate in large clusters, providing a permissive niche for bacterial survival. The switch in macrophage polarization and motility plays an important role in establishing this secure niche for Salmonella.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by imaging data showing bacterial localization in tnfa-negative macrophage clusters (Figures 4, 6). Claims C68, C106, and C108 are logical inferences well-supported by the combined imaging, transcriptomic, and motility data. The conclusion in C109 integrates multiple lines of evidence (polarization switch, reduced motility, bacterial localization) into a coherent model. While some aspects are inferential, they are strongly supported by the experimental data.

result: The zebrafish larva model provides a unique platform for analyzing Salmonella persistent infection and understanding long-term host-pathogen interactions in a whole living animal.
evaluation: Claims C69 and C110 are conclusions supported by the entire body of work presented. The study successfully demonstrates: (1) establishment of persistent infection, (2) real-time visualization of immune cell dynamics, (3) characterization of macrophage polarization states in vivo, (4) transcriptomic profiling of specific cell populations, and (5) analysis of cellular behavior over extended time periods. These capabilities collectively validate the claim that zebrafish provides a unique platform for studying persistent infections.

result: Background claims about Salmonella biology, macrophage polarization, zebrafish as a model system, and prior work on Salmonella-macrophage interactions are established through citations to published literature.
evaluation: Claims C1-C14 and C76-C97, C100 provide background context and are supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed literature. These claims establish the scientific foundation for the current study and accurately represent prior knowledge in the field. The citations appear appropriate and relevant to the claims made.

result: General statements about the importance of understanding host-pathogen interactions, the need for tractable model systems, and gaps in current knowledge regarding macrophage polarization dynamics during Salmonella infection.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are general statements about the field and the rationale for the study. These are reasonable assertions that establish the motivation for the work. C74 and C75 identify specific knowledge gaps that the current study addresses, which is validated by the novelty of the findings presented.

result: Speculative interpretations of unexpected findings, including possible explanations for neuronal gene expression in macrophages (efferocytosis or direct support of neural repair), potential mechanisms underlying reduced macrophage motility (chemokine signaling alterations), and alternative interpretations of transcriptomic dynamics (population changes vs individual cell phenotype switching).
evaluation: Claims C98-C99, C101-C105, C122-C123 are explicitly speculative (using "may" or "might") and represent alternative interpretations of the data rather than definitive conclusions. While these speculations are reasonable and supported by citations where applicable (e.g., C97, C98, C99 cite Lantz et al., 2020), they require additional experimental validation. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than established facts. Future work including single-cell analysis (mentioned in C104-C105) would help resolve these uncertainties.

result: Salmonella persists within aggregates of tnfa-negative macrophages that resemble early granulomas. These structures are characterized as non-epithelioid granulomas initiated by innate immune mechanisms, with macrophages downregulating tight junction genes (cdh1, tjp1a) during persistence.
evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by imaging data showing macrophage aggregates (Figures 4, 6) and RNA-seq data showing downregulation of tight junction genes (C125, Figure 9A). The comparison to granulomas (C124) is reasonable given the structural similarities, though the term "remind" suggests this is interpretive. The characterization as non-epithelioid granulomas (C126) is supported by the gene expression data and comparison with literature on mycobacterial and Salmonella granulomas (C86-C87). However, more detailed structural and functional characterization would strengthen this conclusion.
